title: Kenseiden
subtitle: A samurai crosses the provinces
summary: Kenseiden is Sega's sword-fighting platform adventure, first released for Master System in Japan on 2 June 1988.
body: Kenseiden is Sega's sword-fighting platform adventure, first released for Master System in Japan on 2 June 1988. The samurai Hayato travels through sixteenth-century provinces to recover five scrolls and a sacred sword from hostile warlocks and spirits. Side-view stages provide the individual encounters, placing enemies and obstacles around his movements. The larger journey eventually allows the player to choose the order of provinces, giving the adventure a map to consider beyond the next screen. Its Japanese setting connects the swordplay, creatures and locations into a recognisable supernatural expedition.

Hayato must judge the reach of his sword while moving through the stage's platforms and approaching enemies. Clearing one province contributes to the wider search, but later freedom to choose a destination changes how the journey is organised. Returning to earlier locations also becomes possible before the final stage. The player can therefore treat the map as a set of places to investigate rather than an unbroken line of levels, deciding which route to attempt as the remaining scrolls and the ultimate confrontation draw the expedition onwards.

The side-view action keeps each province immediate, while the map supplies a sense of travelling across a larger country. Distinctive enemies and still scenes reinforce that scale within the Master System's presentation. A South Korean version changed Hayato into a Hwarang warrior and altered the setting, showing how substantially regional presentation could reshape the same underlying game. The original's lasting identity comes from combining a samurai's direct sword attacks with the freedom to revisit provinces, making the task feel like a journey through places with their own dangers and purposes.
